title: Congo Races to Protect Health Workers as Ebola Outbreak Grows
summary:
Health workers in Congo are first in line for a vaccine that could protect them from Ebola. On Saturday, the country began vaccinating doctors, nurses, and other front-line workers in Bunia, the city at the center of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded.

"Our collective duty is to protect life," said Maj. Gen. Gaby Kasongo Mulumba, the military governor of Ituri province. He said these workers are "particularly exposed and deeply involved in the response."

The vaccine is called Ervebo. It worked against a different, more common type of Ebola virus in past outbreaks. But this outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which has no licensed vaccine or treatment. Scientists are still studying whether Ervebo can protect people from Bundibugyo Ebola. The two viruses are related, so there is hope it will help.

About 70,000 doses of Ervebo have been approved for use in Congo. Around 50,000 doses will go to front-line and health workers. The other 20,000 doses will be used in a clinical trial to study whether the vaccine works against Bundibugyo virus.

The campaign in Ituri and North Kivu is expected to reach 20,000 front-line workers over six to nine months.

As of Saturday, Congo had recorded 7,541 confirmed cases, including 3,639 deaths. Another 1,823 people have recovered. The World Health Organization says the outbreak is still out of control and could become the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history.
why_it_matters: When health workers are protected, they can keep caring for sick people — which helps stop a disease from spreading to families and communities far beyond Congo.

background_read: Ebola is a serious disease caused by a virus. It was first discovered in 1976 in Congo, near a river called the Ebola River — that is how it got its name.
The World Health Organization (a health group run by countries around the world) tracks outbreaks and helps send doctors, vaccines and supplies to the places that need them.
Congo (also called the Democratic Republic of the Congo) is a large country in central Africa, and several Ebola outbreaks have started there.
Article_Structure: WHO: Health workers, doctors and nurses in Congo, together with Congo's government and the World Health Organization.
WHAT: Congo began vaccinating front-line health workers with a vaccine called Ervebo.
WHERE: In Bunia, a city in Ituri province in eastern Congo; the campaign covers Ituri and North Kivu.
WHY: To protect the workers who are most exposed to the virus, as the outbreak grows out of control with thousands of cases and deaths.

perspectives.description: Ervebo worked against another type of Ebola in past outbreaks, and because the two viruses are related, researchers hope it can help against Bundibugyo too.
No vaccine or treatment is approved for the Bundibugyo virus yet, so the 20,000 doses being used in a clinical trial are still an experiment, not a proven shield.
The outbreak is the fastest-growing ever recorded and is still out of control, so it could become the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history.
